title: All things new (Revelation 21:5–8)
hookLine: behold, I make all things new

lines: THE ONE ON THE THRONE SPEAKS.
NOT ALL NEW THINGS. ALL THINGS, NEW.
cards: A chipped bowl, glued back together, the crack still showing. A coat with a patch on the elbow. A friendship that broke and then, slowly, didn't.
Mending doesn't swap one thing for another. It's the same thing, made whole. John has just seen a new heaven and a new earth, and a holy city coming down.
Now the one on the throne speaks, and the King James gives the words like this: "Behold, I make all things new." Listen to the order. Not all new things.

teach.b: First, the sentence: "And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new."
Some readers lean on the wording: the old world isn't thrown out while a fresh one is unpacked; the things themselves are made new.
Others hear a cleaner break, since verse one says the first heaven and the first earth "were passed away." Christians hold both readings, and the chapter holds both lines. Second, the tense.

teach.h: I MAKE, NOT I WILL MAKE.
teach.b: The King James says I make, not I will make. Some readers hear it already under way, not only at the end.
Paul writes something close to Corinth: "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." Third, the next breath.
John is told, "Write: for these words are true and faithful."

teach.h: IT IS DONE. ALPHA AND OMEGA.
teach.b: Then: "It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end." The one who started the story finishes it. And a gift: "I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely."
Freely. Thirst is all the verse asks for. Fourth, the hard edge.
Verse eight names the fearful, the unbelieving, murderers, liars and others, and gives them their part in the lake of fire.
Christians read it more than one way: a real judgment, a warning meant to turn people around, or a picture of what can't live in a world made whole.
The passage keeps the promise and the warning side by side.

how: Some churches read Revelation 21 at funerals, and Christians also hear its 'all things new' alongside Paul's words about becoming a new creature in Christ.

o: a fresh start every new year for believers
a new set of laws given to the early church

games.q: you're John. the one on the throne has just said, "behold, I make all things new." what are you told to do next?
o: keep it secret until the end comes.
write it down, for these words are true and faithful.
go and tell the seven churches in person.
games.why: "Write: for these words are true and faithful." then: "It is done. I am Alpha and Omega."

practice: Choose one small thing within reach: a smudged glass, a crooked picture, a message gone stale on your phone. Hold it in your mind and see it made fresh, clean, straight, answered, and notice that it's still itself.
If you pray, hold the words "Behold, I make all things new" in the quiet; if not, just breathe with the one thing you chose.

wordCard.voice: All things new. The promise from the throne in Revelation twenty-one, heard by some readers as the same things made whole, and by others as a fresh start after the old has passed away.

orig.note: Greek: new I make all things. in Revelation 21:5 the word for new comes first.

carryVoice: Your line: all things new. Spoken by the one who started the story. That's today, done.
